title: MC0-09506
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They appeal a negative decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), and ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to substitute a finding that they are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection; in the alternative, they ask that the RAD remit the matter to the RPD for reconsideration.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Principal Appellant), and his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Associate Appellant) are citizens of Nigeria. They appeal with their minor child, XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Minor Appellant) who is a citizen of the United States of America (U.S.A.). They appeal a negative decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), and ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to substitute a finding that they are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection; in the alternative, they ask that the RAD remit the matter to the RPD for reconsideration.

This appeal is allowed in part. In respect of the Principal Appellant and the Associate Appellant, who are citizens of Nigeria and no other country, I send this matter back to the RPD to be redetermined. The determinative issue is credibility, as I have found the RPD erred in its assessment of the Appellants' credibility; however, there remains the open issue of state protection, which ought to be thoroughly reviewed by the RPD on re-determination.

In respect of the Minor Appellant, the RAD agrees with the RPD that she is a citizen of the U.S.A. with no claim advanced against that country.1 This finding was not challenged on appeal. Therefore, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Minor Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Appellants fear persecution from the Ogboni cult members for the Principal Appellant's refusal to become a member and the head of the group. The Appellants allege that members of the Ogboni cult wish to induct the Principal Appellant as a member. Owing to his reluctance to join, the Ogboni made several threatening calls to the Appellants resulting in them seeking the assistance of the police, but they say no help was provided. This lack of police assistance led the Appellants to believe that the Nigerian police were "compromised" by the Ogboni. Consequently, the Appellants went into hiding at a cousin's home located over 2 hours away from their residence in Lagos. However, within hours of arriving at the cousin's home, the Appellants allege they were found and attacked by the Ogboni. Consequently, they fled Nigeria in XXXX 2017 for the U.S.A. and, after having spent eight months in the U.S.A., they entered irregularly into Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, where they made the present claim for refugee protection. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellants is rejected

According to the law,2 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.3

The Appellants have submitted four items they request be admitted as new evidence. These items are:4 a. XXXX Report (in French) for the Associate Appellant, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020; b. Police Report from Nigeria, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020; c. Affidavit from the Principal Appellant's aunt, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020; and d. Photos of damage to Principal Appellant's aunt's home, undated.

The Appellants submit that each of the items arose after the RPD rejected their claim and therefore meet the criteria in subsection 110(4). However, the Appellants, who are represented by counsel, make no submissions on the relevance or credibility of any of the items of new evidence presented.

Subparagraph 3(3)(g)(iii) of the RAD Rules5 requires that an appellant specify how any new documentary evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and how that evidence relates to the appellant. The Appellants, in this case, did not provide full and detailed submissions, or any submissions, about how the new evidence meets the admissibility requirements as it relates to them. It is not for the RAD to do counsel's job for the Appellants, as it is not in the position to make assumptions on what particular portion of any particular document is relevant and how it is relevant to the case at hand. It is the Appellants' job, through counsel, to explain the relevance of the evidence adduced and how the criteria under subsection 110(4) are met. This was not done in this case.

The Appellants likewise make no submissions on the new evidence in their Memorandum, such that, even if admitted, this evidence is not relied on by the Appellants in their appeal. The RAD, therefore, declines to admit their new evidence. Oral hearing request is rejected

The Appellants requested an oral hearing with respect to the new evidence adduced, pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA. When read together, subsections 110(3), (4) and (6) of the IRPA, establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing unless there is new evidence admitted in accordance with the provisions of subsection 110(4), which raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, is central to the RPD's decision and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. Given that no new evidence has been admitted, the Appellants' request for an oral hearing is denied.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.6 Merits of the appeal

The Appellants raise four issues on appeal:7 a. Did the RPD commit a reviewable error by conducting a microscopic analysis of the objective documentary evidence contained in the National Documentation Package? b. Did the RPD commit a reviewable error by failing to address the relevant evidence submitted by the Appellants? c. Did the RPD commit a reviewable error by failing to accord the Principal Appellant an opportunity to respond to its concerns? d. Did the RPD commit a reviewable error in its assessment of the Appellants' credibility?

The RPD found the determinative issue in the Appellants' claim was credibility and found that the presumption of truth had been rebutted, as the Appellants had not credibly established the objective basis for their claim.8 After my own review of the evidence, I agree that this is the determinative issue; as such, the remainder of the Appellants' arguments on this appeal will not be addressed. The objective basis of the Appellants' claim is supported by the documentary evidence

The RPD relied heavily on the objective documentary evidence related to the Ogboni cult,9 which indicated that the Ogboni is "now almost defunct" and that the Ogboni society today "has no power or influence" in finding that the Appellants' failed to establish an objective basis for their claim.10 However, my review of the objective evidence indicates that while some sources indicated the Ogboni are "almost defunct", other sources in the same item indicated that while their influence has not completely disappeared, they have much less importance than in the past, and that the Ogboni are not widespread, compared to other religious movements like Christianity or Islam. It confirms that the Ogboni are regionally located in the six states which make up Yorubaland. It also states that while in general, membership is voluntary, family heritage expectations may result in the use of "force or coercion" if membership is rejected.11 The objective evidence also explicitly refers to and incorporates an earlier item of objective evidence12 which confirms that sources report: ...even though positions within the Ogboni society are not inherited, [i]f one person's parent was a member of the Ogboni Society, and that person had been exposed to their activities (e.g. meetings held at his or her parents' house while the child was present so that over the years the child grew up knowing the identities of the Ogboni; or, the parent deliberately pledged that his or her child would become a member; or, if the child had been used as an assassin by the Ogboni in the sense that he or she had been the "courier" who went into a target's compound and added poison to the water source or whatever), that child would be expected to join. So, in essence only someone who has had a history with them in a very close manner can be intimidated into joining.

This scenario is what the Principal Appellant alleges occurred in his case, where his father had promised the Principal Appellant to the Ogboni society since he was a child. Indeed, the Principal Appellant testified to his own firsthand knowledge from experiences at Ogboni events which he attended with his father from a young age.13 Therefore, I find that the RPD erred in concluding that the objective evidence does not support the Appellants' basis of claim. The RPD erred in impugning the Appellants' credibility

The RPD also used the same item from the documentary evidence to reject the Appellants' explanation for why their evidence differs from the documentary evidence, namely, that there are many factions of the Ogboni,14 which the Appellants argue is in error. I agree. My review of the objective documentary evidence indicates that it explicitly notes that "Ogboni" is a generic term that can refer to several Ogboni societies, while noting the term remains distinct from the Reformed Ogboni Fraternity.15 Therefore, I agree with the Appellants that the RPD erred in rejecting their explanation and impugning their credibility on this basis.

The RPD also found the Principal Appellant's testimony regarding the attack at his wife's cousin's house in Badagry was vague and evasive, citing the fact that the Principal Appellant could not describe the cousin's house where he was staying, and that the Principal Appellant was inconsistent about whether he ran or took a bus from Badagry to a friend's house in Surulere after the attack.16 The Appellants argue these are irrelevant and insignificant details which ought not to undermine their credibility.17

I have reviewed the transcript of the RPD hearing, and note the Principal Appellant gave several specific details about the house in Badagry, including its landscape, that it had no gate, where the guest room was in relation to the bathroom, and the relative size of the home.18 Therefore, I find that the RPD erred when it found the Principal Appellant's testimony on this point was vague and evasive. Likewise, the transcript does not show that the Principal Appellant was inconsistent about how he got from Badagry to Surulere; although he initially explained that after the attack he "ran" to Surelere, which is quite a distance from Badagry, he quickly clarified that he travelled by bus.19 I am satisfied that the Principal Appellant's reference to having "ran" to Surulere was reasonable in the context that he ran to or fled to Surulere, if via bus. I therefore draw no negative inference from the Principal Appellant's testimony on this point. Indeed, my review of the Appellants' testimony does not reveal any inherent inconsistencies or omissions which would undermine their credibility with respect to this central incident which they allege caused them to flee Nigeria.

In light of the totality of the Appellants' evidence and in particular the testimony of both Appellants which was not inconsistent between one another or vis-à-vis their Basis of Claim forms, I do not agree with the RPD in finding that the Appellants failed to credibly establish the objective basis for their claim, or that the negative credibility findings cited by the RPD which arose with respect to the attack at the Associate Appellant's cousin's house, would be sufficient to rebut entirely the presumption of truth to be afforded to the Appellants.20 I agree with the Appellants that the credibility concerns noted were peripheral in nature. According to the transcript, the Appellants' evidence on the alleged persecution and targeting by the Ogboni cult was largely consistent, and therefore I draw no adverse credibility inference. State protection

The RPD had credibility concerns with respect to the Appellants' allegation that the Ogboni have obviously infiltrated the Nigerian police force, on account of the fact that nothing was done in respect of the Appellants' complaint to police, finding that this allegation was "vague and uncorroborated" and noting that there was no objective evidence to support the Appellants' allegation that high-ranking police officers are Ogboni.21 The RPD correctly noted, and I agree, that a review of the documentary evidence confirms there is "no evidence" that the Ogboni have police influence in main cities such as Lagos or Abuja.22 The RPD therefore found the Appellants' allegation that the Nigerian police have been infiltrated by Ogboni members is speculative and not supported by the objective evidence, and that this undermined the Appellants' credibility.23

After conducting my own analysis of the record, I find that the RPD's negative credibility findings are insufficient to maintain its determination that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection; however, I do find the RPD was correct in its assessment that the documentary evidence does not support the Appellants' allegation that the whole of the Nigerian police have been infiltrated by Ogboni cult members, such that the Appellants would be unable to receive state protection in Nigeria, particularly in larger, urban cities where the documents indicate there is "no evidence" that Ogboni members have any influence on the police.24 The RAD is unable to confirm or set aside the RPD's decision without hearing evidence on the issue of whether there is state protection available to them in Nigeria.

As such, the RAD is not in a position to find that the Appellants face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or find, on a balance of probabilities, that they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, or face a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they were to return to Nigeria. Where the RAD is unable to confirm, or set aside and substitute its own decision without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD, paragraph 111(2)(b) of the IRPA allows the RAD to return the case to the RPD for re-determination, which I would do in this case.

Accordingly, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, I would allow this appeal and refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel to consider issues of credibility and whether state protection is available for the Appellants in Nigeria.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Minor Appellant, who is a U.S. citizen with no claim against that country, is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

In respect of the Principal Appellant and the Associate Appellant, the appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel, with direction to consider, inter alia, the issue of state protection.
